blocks.text: The International Center of Photography (ICP) presents “What’s Ms. Pinney Doing Here,” an ongoing project by photographer Melissa Ann Pinney documenting students in the Chicago Public School system. The project is on view in ICP’s Incubator Space, an exhibition program launched in 2025 to highlight the work of emerging photographers responding in real time to the world around us, while pushing the boundaries of the documentary tradition. ICP’s Incubator Space is curated by Sara Ickow, Associate Director of Exhibitions at ICP.

Since 2018, photographer Pinney has documented Chicago Public School students as part of an artist residency. Through a global pandemic, a renewed focus on racial and gender inequities and the persistence of gun violence in Chicago, Pinney photographed at three different schools. This historically significant span of years also became the backdrop to personal losses for these communities: eight students she photographed were shot and killed during the years she was working in the schools. Pinney’s images are a testament to the strong friendships and communities formed in adolescence.

Some students became close collaborators, and through Pinney’s lens we are able to witness how their identities shift and settle through these tender years. As the students began to invite her into their world, the project developed into a document of identity, community and urgent social issues. Pinney’s thoughtful portraits of young people navigating the transformations of adolescence contain all of the triumph, grief, humor and tenderness of growing up.

Melissa Ann Pinney’s work first garnered attention in The Museum of Modern Art’s major 1991 exhibition, Pleasures and Terrors of Domestic Comfort. Her studies of the social lives and emerging identities of American adolescents have earned her many awards, including a Guggenheim Fellowship, three Illinois Arts Council Fellowship Awards and a National Endowment for the Arts Midwest Regional Fellowship. Pinney was selected for three documentary projects that were exhibited, published and archived in Chicago: Changing Chicago (1987), City 2000 and most recently, her work in the Chicago Public Schools. Pinney’s first monograph, Regarding Emma: Photographs of American Women and Girls (2003) was followed by Girl Ascending (2010), TWO (2015) and In Their Own Light: Photographs from Chicago Public Schools (2023).
